Architecture 2.0 is not about prompting language models to write Verilog or automating isolated CAD steps. It is a closed-loop engineering discipline for translating high-level system intent into physically verified silicon: systematically exploring hardware–software trade-offs, qualifying evidence through physical checks against strong non-learned baselines, and maintaining nondelegable human commitment authority.

Learned methods can search high-dimensional spaces faster than a designer can enumerate them, fit empirical patterns where no analytical model is available, and propose candidate structures a designer would not have drafted. Applying those capabilities to computer systems and silicon chip design is one of the most unforgiving tests they face. An architectural decision begins with high-level software intent and cascades through compilers, instruction set architectures, microarchitectures, and register-transfer level (RTL) netlists down to physical silicon signoff. Along this path, empirical observations are expensive, noisy, and inherently partial. Compilers, cycle-level simulators, formal verification engines, and post-layout timing tools each expose a narrow slice of system behavior under conflicting assumptions. Worse still, the cost of error in hardware is asymmetric. While software can be patched in production, a timing glitch or coherence bug discovered after mask tapeout costs tens of millions of dollars in mask respins and delays a product by months.

That asymmetric penalty defines both the danger and the opportunity of automated design. Generative models can draft candidate RTL and architectural variations far faster than physical toolchains can evaluate them. But proposing alternatives creates engineering value only when the system can qualify what those alternatives physically achieve. An *AI-native design system* does not bolt machine-learning models onto existing scripts; it rebuilds the exploration loop around the tools that return evidence. It unites learned surrogates, deterministic simulators, and physical signoff engines around machine-usable state representations, systematically resolving hardware and software trade-offs under an explicit verification budget.

Pursuing that closed loop is what led Amir Yazdanbakhsh and me to formulate the Architecture 2.0 moonshot in our initial paper [@ReddiYazdanbakhsh2025Architecture20]. At the time, proposing that automated, closed-loop exploration could fundamentally reshape how chips and systems are designed met with candid skepticism across the computer architecture community. To many colleagues, treating complex microarchitectural exploration as an automated, learned search problem sounded impractical, if not fanciful.

Today, that skepticism has given way to rapid adoption of machine learning across the semiconductor industry. Teams deploy generative models to accelerate logic drafting, while learned optimizers tune placement macros and compute kernels inside closed loops. Yet optimizing an isolated task or searching within a frozen subsystem container is not the same as building an AI-native design system. Current practice remains fundamentally constrained. Even where local loops run automatically, human architects must still manually bridge disconnected tools, partition subsystem boundaries, and absorb the verification burden when candidate designs fail.

The ambition of this book extends past isolated point assistance and bounded subsystem optimization. The question is whether a complete, closed-loop design system can find better architectures, reduce the engineering cost of finding them, or do both. I wrote this book to make that possibility concrete without assuming its success. The chapters establish the principles, state representations, and execution harnesses required to pursue the moonshot without mistaking local code generation for full-system success.

The architectural problem always comes first. Depending on the physical constraints, the right engineering choice may combine learned surrogates, heuristic optimization, formal proofs, or conventional analysis with no machine learning at all. Architecture 2.0 is not a dogma claiming that every circuit demands an AI model; it is a discipline for determining where AI earns its place and what physical evidence its recommendations must deliver.

## On the Title of This Book {.unnumbered}

The title of this book, *Architecture 2.0: Principles of AI-Native System and Chip Design*, is a compact declaration of its scope, where each term establishes a deliberate boundary. Architecture 2.0 names two things this book keeps apart. It names a shift in how architecture work is done: the transition from manual, intuition-driven point sweeps toward automated, closed-loop exploration across the full hardware–software stack. It also names the discipline that shift demands, which is what the chapters teach. The shift is a claim the book defends rather than takes on faith, and the discipline is what makes the claim checkable. I chose *Principles* because specific model weights and tool scripts are transient, whereas the underlying physics, evidence standards, and architectural trade-offs outlast them.

*AI-native* carries a precise technical meaning in this work. As defined above, it is the transition from bolting point-assistance models onto isolated computer-aided design (CAD) tasks, to constructing the entire exploration workflow, state representations, and verification harnesses around automated search. Finally, *System and Chip Design* names the physical reality that a silicon floorplan cannot be optimized in isolation from the software workloads, compiler lowering passes, memory hierarchies, and thermal constraints that govern its behavior.

## What This Book Teaches {.unnumbered}

To anchor its principles in concrete physical constraints, this book develops a recurring case study: a real-time mobile extended-reality (XR) compute subsystem operating under a strict 3\ W thermal design power budget and tight area limits. The prospective Lighthouse study is the anchor used to trace an architectural hypothesis through the evidence an engineering claim would require. The chapters develop its governing question around this 3\ W limit, construct a machine-usable representation of design state, and identify the methods and deterministic tool executions needed to evaluate proposed candidates. The focus stays on the physical mechanisms and trade-offs that architects must judge rather than on the transient syntax of any individual tool.

Evaluating whether an automated workflow improves a design program requires scrutinizing the entire human-and-tool system. A fluent generative model inside a broken verification loop accelerates the production of invalid silicon. Conversely, a modest, well-calibrated surrogate that eliminates a weeks-long simulation bottleneck can change a tapeout schedule. Every method in this book faces two questions. *Did the complete approach improve the architecture result, or reduce the total cost of reaching a comparable one, against a credible alternative?* And *should a named authority commit physical silicon to the result?* The first question is technical and measurable. The second is an organizational judgment that a person makes and owns.

Answering those questions means moving past isolated point tools to govern the whole exploration life cycle. The reader learns to formulate the question and represent the design state, to connect methods to real tools and qualify what those tools return, and to evaluate the complete approach and own the commitment that follows. Those three moves are what one team can perform with the tools it already has. The book then changes altitude once, at the end, to ask which of the limits such a team reaches are shared across the discipline rather than local to that team.

The Lighthouse study opens with intent formulation in @sec-moonshot, formalizes state representations and tool interfaces in @sec-data-representations-world-models and @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces, and returns in @sec-what-architect-owns to state what the book's records do and do not justify. Its own execution path stops before dispatch: @sec-architecture-20-ontology and @sec-what-architect-owns examine what an honest stop looks like when prerequisites remain incomplete, while @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization and @sec-feedback-verification-trust examine empirical systolic-array evaluations that ran their budgets to completion. The companion hands-on laboratories execute these loops directly. Nothing in this subsystem can be settled in isolation. The power envelope constrains the accelerator, the accelerator reshapes memory traffic, and the memory hierarchy shifts thermal hot spots across the die. Holding the Lighthouse study to the same admission criteria the book asks of the field is how it shows what an honest stop looks like, with unresolved risks kept as open questions rather than claimed as victories.

Architecture 2.0 sits at the intersection of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation (EDA; @fig-book-composition). Each overlap already has a field of work behind it. Architecture and machine learning help us predict performance and search large design spaces. Architecture and EDA connect system choices to RTL and physical implementation. Machine learning and EDA are already changing synthesis, placement, routing, and verification. What we are after sits where all three meet.

![**Architecture 2.0 unifies computer architecture, machine learning, and EDA.** Computer architecture supplies the questions and design trade-offs, machine learning supplies methods for learning and search, and EDA supplies executable implementation and analysis tools together with physical evidence or estimates. Work at their intersection must satisfy the relevant standards of all three.](images/fig-book-composition){#fig-book-composition width="100%" fig-alt="Three-circle Venn diagram of computer architecture, machine learning, and electronic design automation, with Architecture 2.0 at their intersection."}

Work at that intersection has to satisfy all three fields at once. A generated artifact that ignores the workload is not an architecture result. A promising estimate that cannot survive implementation is not a physical result. A successful tool run without a fair comparison does not show that AI improved the work.

The scope of automation matters when judging such claims. Helping with one task, optimizing a subsystem within fixed interfaces, and searching across system boundaries demand different capabilities and checks. @sec-moonshot develops this distinction through three operational layers; the moonshot pursues the broadest scope all the way to physically verified silicon. This book is not a catalog of transient neural architectures, a prompt-engineering recipe, or a defense of unconstrained automation. I do not argue that heuristics should replace architectural judgment or formal verification. Physical signoff checks remain decisive, and named human architects remain accountable for every committed tapeout.

## The Discipline of Design Principles {.unnumbered}

Machine-learning models and EDA scripts change every month, and the prompts and wrappers written for them go stale with them. What lasts is a principle rooted in semiconductor physics, the cost of a measurement, and documented failures. A true architectural principle will still govern the silicon outcome even if model capability grows by orders of magnitude and inference cost falls to zero.

The principles in this book are introduced alongside the specific technical problems that demand them. Each chapter states one or two as callouts, and each part page lists the principles its chapters carry, mapping each rule to the failure it predicts and the review question that makes it inspectable. The companion @sec-appendix-b-laws-paradoxes gathers the borrowed laws and paradoxes the chapters invoke, from Amdahl's law to the optimizer's curse, providing a quick reference for derivations.

## Who This Book Is For {.unnumbered}

The primary audience is the practicing computer architect, chip designer, and systems researcher. I assume familiarity with performance, power, area, and hardware–software interfaces, alongside working literacy in engineering software (Python, C++, or standard hardware description languages). No prior background in deep learning is required; the machine-learning ideas the argument needs are introduced where they are used, through concrete architecture problems and physical constraints.

Because Architecture 2.0 bridges traditionally isolated silos, the text addresses four technical communities:

- **Computer architects** seeking to integrate automated search and generative models into design exploration without loosening the physical checks that make a result trustworthy.
- **EDA and CAD engineers** looking to connect synthesis, placement, and verification toolchains to high-level architectural decision loops.
- **Machine learning and ML-systems researchers** entering hardware design who need to understand how physical signoff, evaluation costs, and formal verification redefine what constitutes a valid result.
- **Graduate students and engineering leaders** spanning hardware and software who need a framework and a shared vocabulary for governing AI-native systems engineering.

## How to Read This Book {#book-structure .unnumbered}

This book is organized into four cumulative parts that follow an architectural study from initial intent to physical signoff and organizational commitment:

- **Part I: System Intent and Design Life Cycles** analyzes the physical scaling limits and economic pressures breaking manual design loops and introduces the six-stage design life cycle (Formulate, Explore, Implement, Evaluate, Interpret, and Commit), grounded in the running Lighthouse mobile XR moonshot.
- **Part II: Technical Building Blocks** constructs the engineering infrastructure of Architecture 2.0: structured state representations, smallest sufficient methods, isolated tool harnesses, and the qualification of returned signals before they drive any action.
- **Part III: Operation, Evaluation, and Ownership** analyzes cross-stack pattern transfer, applies adversarial red-teaming and matched-budget evaluation, and establishes nondelegable human commitment authority, while companion laboratories provide executable environments for closed-loop sweeps.
- **Part IV: Open Infrastructure and Ecosystems** charts the precompetitive schemas, open process design kits, grand challenges, and university curricula needed to sustain an open research ecosystem.

Reading sequentially gives the complete engineering argument, and each of the four communities above can also enter through the chapters closest to its own work (@tbl-reading-paths). Three chapters form the spine every path shares: the moonshot and its evidence standard (@sec-moonshot), the life cycle that organizes the work (@sec-architecture-20-ontology), and the commitment decision that ends it (@sec-what-architect-owns).

| **Reader** | **Start with** | **Then** |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Computer architect | @sec-moonshot, @sec-design-loop-no-longer-scales, @sec-architecture-20-ontology | @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack, @sec-what-architect-owns |
| EDA and CAD engineer | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-architecture-environments-tool-interfaces | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-loop-patterns-across-stack |
| Machine learning researcher | @sec-data-representations-world-models, @sec-methods-generation-prediction-optimization | @sec-feedback-verification-trust, @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect |
| Graduate student or engineering leader | @sec-moonshot, @sec-architecture-20-ontology | @sec-evaluating-agentic-architect, @sec-what-architect-owns, @sec-bootstrapping-ecosystem |
: **Four reading paths through the same argument.** EDA developers and ML researchers gain most from the state representations and execution harnesses of Part II; architects and engineering leaders gain most from the execution, evaluation, and governance chapters of Part III. Every path passes through the moonshot, the life cycle, and the commitment decision. {#tbl-reading-paths tbl-colwidths="[24,38,38]"}

While the entries in @tbl-reading-paths tailor entry points to distinct technical roles, they converge on the same core thesis. EDA engineers and machine learning researchers will find immediate traction in the state representations and isolated tool harnesses of Part II, whereas silicon architects and engineering leads can focus on the operational evaluation, pattern transfer, and commitment criteria of Part III. Regardless of background, however, every path requires confronting the evidence standards established across the three spine chapters.

As you read, test these principles against a live design problem in your own work. Ask which decision matters, what hidden physical constraints must be exposed, which baseline comparison is fair, what the tools actually measured, and what risks remain unverified. The measure of this book is whether its principles carry to design problems it never mentions.

Specific neural architectures, benchmark leaderboards, and EDA tool application programming interfaces will continue to change. The reasoning in this book is built to outlast them. A team that grounds its automated design work in problem formulation, explicit state representation, tool discipline, adversarial evaluation, and human commitment authority can adopt new models without rebuilding its method each time.

I expect artificial intelligence to change how architects design chips and systems. Whether it does depends on the discipline taking that prospect seriously without taking anyone's claims on faith, mine included. Generating code is not that change. The change, if it comes, will come from design systems that carry intent to checked physical results and from architects with the judgment to govern them. Architecture 2.0 is the discipline for deciding where AI belongs, where it does not, and what the evidence shows.
